types: one CLR public type identity maps to one Ruby constant identity
constructors: retain every .ctor identity; dispatch through initialize
overloads: retain every CLR signature identity in the static contract

refOut.refInput: ordinary typed Ruby value input copied at value boundaries
refOut.multipleOut: ordered Array following any non-void CLR return
refOut.singleOutWithReturn: ordered Array of [return value, out value]; the CLR fills its out parameter on every branch, so neither half of the result is dropped

arrayTransforms: caller-owned source/destination Arrays; whole and indexed range forms preserve forward overlap order

collections.genericICollection: preserve the CLR interface identity and project its selected typed members directly on the Ruby collection class
collections.genericIEnumerable: preserve the CLR interface identity; GetEnumerator returns Ruby Enumerator without a fake System namespace
collections.enumerationMutation: fail-fast when the backing collection version changes
collections.indexErrors: a collection index outside 0...Count raises Ruby IndexError, the identity Array#fetch raises, and it is out of range rather than counting from the end; a CopyTo whose destination cannot hold the source raises ArgumentError. CurveKeyCollection established both and every projected collection follows them, so one CLR operation keeps one Ruby behaviour across the binding. This is narrower than the thrownExceptions table's ArgumentOutOfRangeException -> RangeError, which covers a CLR exception a projected member's own IL constructs and rethrows; a collection indexer's out-of-range condition belongs to the backing list, not to the member

staticMembers: class methods; struct-valued members return fresh objects

System.IntPtr.validation: inclusive signed range derived from Fiddle::SIZEOF_VOIDP
System.IntPtr.nativeBoundary: two's-complement bit pattern in the canonical fixed-width C carrier; never Fiddle::Pointer

structs: Ruby classes with boundary copies and dup/clone; assignment aliasing is documented
operators: map to Ruby syntax where available and retain op_* identity in static contract

events.identity: one CLR public event maps to one public Ruby event reader keeping the XNA spelling; never an add_Name/remove_Name pair, never a writer, never a Proc, Array or callback property
events.support: the reader answers the generic CNA::Runtime::Event subscription primitive, whose whole public surface is add/remove
events.subscribe: add(callable) or add { |sender, args| ... } appends one handler and answers the token remove takes back; duplicate subscriptions are permitted
events.unsubscribe: remove(handler) removes the last matching occurrence, as Delegate.Remove does to a multicast invocation list; removing an absent handler is harmless
events.dispatch: registration order, over a snapshot, with exceptions never swallowed
events.raise: internal to the declaring implementation; no consumer-facing emit, fire, trigger or call exists
events.abstract: on an XNA interface contract the event reader raises NotImplementedError like every other member: an interface declares the identity and never owns an invocation list

generics.contract: retain CLR arity/signature and reject ambiguous runtime dispatch
generics.runtimeTypeName: each CLR generic type definition Name`N maps deterministically to NameOfT for arity 1 and NameOfT1T2...TN for higher arity
generics.collisionRule: the non-generic CLR identity keeps Name; no alias may collapse it with the generic identity
generics.methodProjection: a CLR generic method projects to a Ruby method taking its type arguments as leading positional parameters, in declaration order, ahead of the CLR value parameters, so the Ruby arity is genericParameters.length + parameters.length. Ruby has no static generics and cannot infer a type argument from a call site, so the type argument must be a value; System.Type already projects to Module, so it is a Ruby Module. This is a rule the verifier can check rather than a per-method choice, and it is the only reason a projected Ruby method may take more arguments than the CLR signature declares.
generics.parameterPlaceholder: !!N names a generic method parameter and !N a generic type parameter, either optionally as an array. Both are language constructs rather than type identities: they are resolved by methodProjection and by the projects_elements metadata respectively, and neither is ever an unmapped BCL type.

expectedMemberFormula: reference public members minus enum value__ metadata storage

bclProjection.register: CNA::Runtime::BclProjection; measured, not aspirational — the API verifier resolves every entry and the dependency frontier consumes the same register
bclProjection.namespace: a projected BCL identity lives in the CNA runtime; no fabricated Ruby ::System namespace is created
bclProjection.scope: only a CLR identity the selected XNA surface actually names, and whose Ruby projection can be decided without guessing, is admitted

exceptions.principle: an XNA exception must behave as a Ruby exception rather than an ordinary Object subclass
exceptions.root: StandardError, because a CLR catch (Exception) is the analogue of a bare Ruby rescue; ::Exception would put XNA failures alongside Ruby's non-recoverable system-level conditions
exceptions.intermediateBases: an intermediate BCL exception class the selected XNA surface never names collapses to the nearest projected ancestor; no Ruby constant is invented for it

thrownExceptions.policy: a CLR exception a projected member throws maps to the nearest Ruby exception with the same meaning, and one CLR exception always maps to exactly one Ruby exception
thrownExceptions.System.ArgumentNullException: ArgumentError; the CLR throws it for a null *or empty* string, so TypeError would be wrong for half its cases
thrownExceptions.System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException: RangeError, the same class this binding already raises for a value outside its allowed range
thrownExceptions.System.NotSupportedException: CNA::Runtime::NotSupportedError, a dedicated language-support class that descends from StandardError. Ruby's NotImplementedError is deliberately refused: it descends from ScriptError, not StandardError, so a bare rescue -- the analogue of a CLR catch (Exception) -- would not catch it, and a routine recoverable CLR failure would escape ordinary Ruby error handling. RuntimeError and ArgumentError are catchable but each say something the CLR exception does not and neither carries a distinct identity a caller can rescue by name. The admitted mscorlib settles the hierarchy (SystemException under System.Exception, which this register already roots at StandardError) and the three public constructors; the parameterless form's CLR message is the localized framework resource Arg_NotSupportedException, which is not reproduced, so a NotSupportedError raised without a message carries Ruby's own default
thrownExceptions.System.InvalidOperationException: RuntimeError, Ruby's generic recoverable failure and the class raise "message" produces, paired with the CLR's generic wrong-state failure. The binding was already pairing them before this register existed: CurveKeyCollection raises RuntimeError for the fail-fast enumeration the CLR signals with InvalidOperationException, and ReadOnlyCollection follows it. FrozenError would say something about frozen objects the CLR does not, and StandardError itself would lose the identity
thrownExceptions.System.Collections.Generic.KeyNotFoundEx: KeyError, Ruby's own "the key was not found in this keyed collection" identity and what Hash#fetch raises. Dictionary`2::get_Item constructs it through ThrowHelper::ThrowKeyNotFoundException when FindEntry answers a negative index; KeyError descends from IndexError and so from StandardError, and reusing it keeps the distinction the CLR draws between a missing index and a missing key, which System.IndexOutOfRangeException already occupies in this table
thrownExceptions.System.Runtime.Serialization.Serializati: CNA::Runtime::SerializationError, a dedicated StandardError subclass for the same reason NotSupportedError is one. SerializationInfo really throws it twice -- Serialization_SameNameTwice when AddValue is given a name already present, and Serialization_NotFound when GetElement cannot find one -- and no existing Ruby class says what it says: RuntimeError is already spoken for by InvalidOperationException and would lose the identity, and KeyError would claim a keyed collection this is not
thrownExceptions.whoConstructsItDecides: this table maps a CLR exception the projected member's own IL constructs -- an ldstr naming a parameter followed by a newobj, or a call into a throw helper. A condition that arises in this binding's own Ruby backing container instead, because the CLR member merely forwards to its backing IList<T>, is governed by collections.indexErrors and raises IndexError; no CLR exception is being projected there. TouchCollection's indexer constructs ArgumentOutOfRangeException("index") itself and therefore raises RangeError, while ReadOnlyCollection and CurveKeyCollection forward and therefore raise IndexError

bclProjection.authority: a BCL identity with a real member surface is measured from the pinned Microsoft .NET Framework mscorlib admitted by tools/api_compat/reference/BCL_PROVENANCE.md, never recalled. The measured surface and its derived behavioural facts live in docs/generated/bcl-inventory.json
bclProjection.genericProjection: a projected CLR generic definition answers for every constructed form of itself: ReadOnlyCollection`1[X] resolves to the same Ruby class as ReadOnlyCollection`1. A Ruby class is not statically generic, so the CLR type arguments cannot live in the superclass expression and are carried as class metadata instead, declared with projects_elements and measured by the API verifier under GENERIC_MAPPING_MISMATCH
bclProjection.readOnlyCollection: System.Collections.ObjectModel.ReadOnlyCollection`1 projects to the dedicated support class CNA::Runtime::ReadOnlyCollection, never to Array, a frozen Array, Enumerable alone, Set or an opaque Object. The mscorlib IL settles why: the CLR constructor stores the IList<T> reference and every public read member forwards one call to it, so the wrapper is a live view and a frozen copy would be a different type; the six read members validate nothing of their own; and read-only is a property of the interface, expressed by twelve explicit interface implementations whose whole body throws NotSupportedException unconditionally, which in Ruby is projected as the absence of any mutating member. An XNA class whose CLR base is this generic inherits from the support class, because Ruby has class inheritance and flattening the inherited surface into unrelated methods would lose the CLR base relationship
bclProjection.collection: System.Collections.ObjectModel.Collection`1 projects to the dedicated support class CNA::Runtime::Collection, never to Array, and it is the mutable sibling of the read-only projection rather than a second design. The mscorlib IL shows one shape with two intents: both classes store a single IList<T> field, both forward every read to it, neither copies anything. This one's mutating members are ordinary public members, and not one of them touches the backing list -- Add, Insert, Item[]=, Remove, RemoveAt and Clear each validate and then call one of four protected virtual hooks, InsertItem, RemoveItem, SetItem or ClearItems. That indirection is what the type is for, so the projection declares no Ruby-idiomatic mutation beside the CLR surface: a << or a push would be a second way to mutate that a subclass's hook never sees. Two constructors answer differently and both are kept: the parameterless one creates its own backing list, the IList<T> one refuses null naming list and otherwise stores the reference. Every mutating member reads items.IsReadOnly first and throws NotSupportedException when it holds, which for a Ruby backing Array is Array#frozen?; the three index-taking writers bound-check only after that, so the refusal is observable ahead of the range error. The reads validate nothing and raise IndexError under collections.indexErrors, while the three writers construct ArgumentOutOfRangeException naming index in their own bodies and raise RangeError -- whoConstructsItDecides, visible on both sides of one type
bclProjection.languageSupport: a support class may carry Ruby-idiomatic identities beside the CLR ones, and they are not XNA identities. CNA::Runtime::ReadOnlyCollection declares each, the single Ruby identity that carries CLR GetEnumerator, and includes Enumerable, every method of which Ruby derives from each alone. The two sets are separable by construction: a CLR identity is PascalCase or an operator, language support is not
bclProjection.notSupportedProjection: CNA::Runtime::NotSupportedError is a BCL projection, not an XNA type, and it is the only exception class in the CNA runtime namespace. It exists because six TouchCollection identities and the CLR read-only collection contract throw System.NotSupportedException, and because no built-in Ruby exception carries that meaning without either escaping a bare rescue or losing the identity
bclProjection.systemTypeProjection: System.Type is a type token everywhere the selected XNA surface names it -- a service key, a content reader's target type, an index element type, a converter's destination -- in all twenty-four places. Ruby's type token is a Module, and a Class is one. The single operation any of those members performs on it, IsAssignableFrom(value.GetType()), is exactly value.is_a?(type), and a Module used as a Hash key compares by identity, which is what Dictionary<Type, ...>'s default comparer does. Nothing claims the CLR Type reflection surface
bclProjection.structuralCollapse: a BCL identity the selected XNA surface names that projects to no Ruby constant at all, recorded in CNA::Runtime::BclProjection::STRUCTURAL_COLLAPSE with its reason. Ruby has no interfaces, so a BCL interface whose whole declared surface the implementing XNA type already exposes publicly survives as those members; inventing a Ruby module would add an identity the CLR contract does not have and that nothing could measure. System.IServiceProvider is the first entry: one member, GetService(Type), which GameServiceContainer declares publicly. System.IDisposable is the second and the one with real reach: the admitted mscorlib shows it declares exactly one member, void Dispose(), and nothing else -- no Close, no IsDisposed, no finalizer contract, no ownership protocol, all of which are conventions built on top of it. Twenty-nine XNA types declare it, twenty-eight declare a public parameterless Dispose() of their own, and the twenty-ninth implements it explicitly, which projects to no member under the same rule ReadOnlyCollection and Collection follow. Mapping the identity is a statement about the interface and about nothing else: it does not claim any type's disposal is implemented, and it does not make a native runtime available. The API verifier asserts that no constant was invented after all, so the entry is a checked decision rather than a note

constructorFreeClasses: a CLR class whose only constructor is internal projects to a Ruby class with `new` made private, as GraphicsResource and Texture already do; its public non-constructibility is part of the contract and the internal construction path stays reachable to a future producer through __send__. No producer is fabricated, and no public Ruby constructor is created that XNA does not expose.
